en: In the *Jinpi* (The Golden Scalpel), the Venerable Chan Master Shanhui, the abbot of Jiahe Yuxi Changle Jiao Temple, evaluates the meaning of "insentient beings possess Buddha-nature" as explained therein. Upon first encountering this doctrine, he remarked:

"I was unaware that insentient beings have nature. (The character for "unaware," *bujue*, is pronounced with the second tone, *yù*. This concludes the section on the Buddha-nature of insentient beings.
At the end, he said: "Suddenly, like awakening from a dream, there is nothing at all to be gained from what was asked or answered.

Because the masters of previous generations saw only the beginning and end of his sleep-talking, they did not discern it. Recently, there has been one who composed the *Xianxing lu* (Record of Manifesting the Nature) or provided commentaries on it.
Mencius said: "You are truly a man of Qi; you know only Guan Zhong and Yanzi."
The *Jinbi* states: "I am a rustic guest; my appearance is coarse and rugged, and my movements lack constancy. When approaching, I stand level with you.
It further says: "Thereupon the rustic guest withdrew respectfully and knelt at an angle."
The critique states: Are those who utter such words sages or ordinary people? A sage must have forgotten emotions; "emotion" is the hallmark of an ordinary person.
Even if one were to offer refutations, one should maintain propriety and ritual decorum (*li-yue*). If there were principles worth adopting, others would naturally submit to them.

How can one, based on the intensity of one's own passions or the loftiness of one’s competitive spirit, judge right and wrong, considering oneself right and others wrong, praising oneself and disparaging others—as if one were Xianshou (Xuanzang)?
The preface to the *Ten Houses of Established Teachings* states: "All of them were Dharma generals of their time, whose brilliant awakening was peerless;

they served as luminous models through successive generations, and their stages of attainment are unfathomable. For instance, Master Si and Master Zhizhe manifested supernatural wonders and spiritual resonance;
their traces reached the ranks of the [Bodhisattva] stages, and their hearing of the Dharma at Vulture Peak remains vivid even today. Qingliang cites the *Biography of Wei Xuzhou*.
It is said that since the Buddhist teachings flowed eastward, the Secret [Mantra] has been elucidated; this was realized by Master Zhiyi (Siming Zhizhe) and propagated by Master Zhanran (Zhendi).
Thus, when Master Zhanran saw it for the first time, he remarked: "In days past at Vulture Peak, we heard the Lotus Sūtra together;
pursued by our karmic affinity from those former lives, you have come here once again. Therefore, one knows the difficulty of being a creator; how could there be room for even a single [error]?
As for your dismissal of other schools as being erroneous, although I am not quick-witted, I shall provide a brief analysis to offer a partial clarification, so that they may attain self-awakening.
The *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel) states:
A guest said, "I have the honor of seeking the Buddhist teachings and have studied their fundamental sources to some extent; how could my extensive exposition of this school be in error?"
At the twin trees, in his final utterance, the Buddha proclaimed the ultimate discourse, stating that "Buddha-nature does not refer to insentient things.

Why, then, do you alone claim that insentient things possess Buddha-nature? I answer: It is because you are not conversant with the teachings on whether Buddha-nature is present or absent, nor with the provisional and the real among the various scriptural divisions.

This causes you to doubt it like an ordinary person. For now, I shall extensively cite the scriptural texts for your sake, so that those of future generations who delight in the Dharma may [understand].
Citing this passage to prove that the Buddha-nature is not insentient (*niṣceṣṭa*) correctly captures the intent of the sutra.
In the thirty-first chapter, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, it says: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space; it is neither internal nor external.

If it were either internal or external, how could it be called 'existing everywhere'? Observe the single character 'existence' (*asti*): what does empty space not encompass? It further states: "It is neither..."
"Buddha-nature" refers to walls, tiles, and stones; thus we know that the scriptural passage relies on expedient teaching to speak of it.

Furthermore, the subsequent text states, "As Kāśyapa has cited, all three exist"; this is because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks from the perspective of provisional gates, and therefore the Buddha accords with Kāśyapa by stating that all three exist.

The commentary states: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says that "Buddha-nature" is termed "the emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and this "emptiness of the ultimate truth" is termed "wisdom.
These two are non-dual, and thus constitute Buddha-nature. Now, while the emptiness of the ultimate truth is Buddha-nature, the nature [of that emptiness] is termed wisdom;
this is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Buddha-nature. The emptiness of the ultimate truth does not exist apart from wisdom; it is merely designated as such.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is called Buddha-nature by virtue of its presence within wisdom.

If one considers the nature from the perspective of its manifestations, then only sentient beings possess Buddha-nature because they possess wisdom; walls, tiles, and rubble lack Buddha-nature because they lack wisdom.

However, if one considers the manifestations from the perspective of the nature—that is, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā), which is omnipresent—then even walls and the like are [all Buddha-nature].

Regarding the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), why is it not a substantial nature? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One knows that all phenomena are the very self-nature of the mind.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because the nature of form is identical to the nature of wisdom, the essence of form is formless and is called the Wisdom Body (*jñāna-kāya*);
because the nature of wisdom is identical to the nature of form, it is called the Dharma Body (*dharma-kāya*), which pervades all places as the luminous essence."

Originally, [the teachings] were uniform; now, because their nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are distinguished, they are divided into two meanings. How can you then ask why we speak of the provisional and the real (upāya-tattva) within the divisions of the teachings?

Nevertheless, there are unequal distinctions regarding the existence or non-existence of the spiritual lineage (gotra), as well as the false and the correct, the Great and the Small, and the provisional and the real.

For example, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon that "spontaneity" (svayambhū) is the cause capable of producing all things; this is a false cause. If one were to claim that all things arise spontaneously...
That the whiteness of a crane and the blackness of a crow arise [spontaneously] would mean they are without cause; to have no cause or a false cause constitutes a great error.
Regarding the six types of *gotra* (spiritual lineages) in the Hīnayāna, within the sixth, the immovable (*akopya*), there are three grades:
the superior is the Buddha-lineage, the middling is the Pratyekabuddha-lineage, and the inferior is the Śrāvaka-lineage. Although this is explained therein...
The Buddha alone possesses the lineage of Buddhahood (*buddhagotra*), yet this is not the nature of his Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This is because, regarding the Buddha’s qualities, it is not said that he gives rise to great activity until the end of the future;

thus, one should know that within the Hīnayāna, with the exception of the Buddha alone, all other sentient beings are not said to possess the nature of Great Enlightenment, as stated in the Hīnayāna treatises.
If the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna establishes the lineage (*gotra*) within conditioned and impermanent phenomena, it cannot encompass all five types of lineages among sentient beings;
thus, there would be a portion of sentient beings who lack the lineage. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Xianyang lun) states:
"What are the distinctions of lineage? There are five principles, namely: the distinction of all realms (*dhātu*)."
Because they can be attained, one should know that all sentient beings possess five types of lineage (*gotra*).

As for the fifth type of lineage, because it lacks the causes for supramundane merit, it never attains *nirvāṇa*. Based on the three roots of goodness, the lineages of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are established.
If one practices any one of the three types of conduct but has not yet reached the fundamental stage, one is established as having an indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
If one establishes the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) based on the fact that the three types of practice have not been fully cultivated at all—
as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that among the three kinds of people, those who will ultimately die are likened to *icchantikas* who lack Buddha-nature—
then, according to the Mahāyāna’s True Teaching (*saddharma*), since the lineage (*gotra*) is established within the very nature of *tathatā*, it exists universally in all sentient beings.
Regarding the nature [of things], the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "White stone has the nature of silver; yellow stone has the nature of gold;

water has the nature of moisture; fire has the nature of heat; likewise, all sentient beings possess the nature of *nirvāṇa*. As the Sūtra says: 'Sentient beings are also thus; they all possess a mind.
All who possess a mind will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is entirely so.
Regarding this meaning, the *Wenying zhilun* (Treatise on Wisdom Derived from Hearing) states: "That which exists within the category of sentient beings is called Buddha-nature;
that which exists outside the category of sentient beings is called Dharma-nature. Did he truly read the treatise thoroughly and examine it minutely?

For nowhere in the treatise is such a statement found. How could he have read the treatise so personally? Furthermore, [Zhiyi] himself composed the *Miaole* (Sublime Joy), where he explains the four lines of text and meaning as follows: one...
That which possesses both form and meaning is used by ordinary people; that which lacks form but possesses meaning is used by the wise.
If the *Wenmiao* (Equal and Wondrous Joy) were truly the *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel), it certainly would not be so; if the *Jinbi* were truly the *Wenmiao*, it certainly would not be so.
An ancient said: "I shall buy your spear and turn it against your shield. Whether it penetrates or does not penetrate, there will be no words to offer. If [the two were] one...
The lineage of the vehicle’s teaching is profoundly deep; its cause and fruit are non-dual, universally relying upon and correctly exhausting the three periods of time.
It encompasses all phenomena—principle, matter, understanding, and practice—and is primordially fulfilled and already perfected.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The bodhisattva lineage is profoundly deep and vast, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space. This...
This is what is meant. How much more so in the *Avataṃsaka*, where the ocean of nature, the cloud-platforms, and the jeweled nets all together proclaim the wondrous sound;
where the light from every pore can preach the Dharma; where fragrant clouds and trees are themselves the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm;

and where lands and sentient beings are fundamentally the true embodiment of the ten bodies. How could anything not be the nature? Thus, the Great Sutra says: "The lands speak, and sentient beings speak."

The *Tri-sahasra-sarva-buddha-vyākaraṇa* (or similar texts) further states: "All realms of the various worlds are all capable of causing the turning of the Wheel of Dharma," and such passages are not few. Question:

Since this is so, why is it that when it exists within the category of sentient beings (*sattva-gaṇa*) it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), while when it exists within the category of non-sentient things (*asattva-gaṇa*) it is called Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)? Each [school] asserts its own position based on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). As it is said: [The following passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* follows: "Regarding the nature of the Tathāgata, there are two aspects: first, the aspect of being the basis for the manifestation of the Tathāgata; second, the aspect of being the object of the Tathāgata’s realization. The first refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as the support for the arising of the Tathāgata’s body. The second refers to the True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the object of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the same in all Buddhas and all sentient beings; there is no difference whatsoever. However, because of the presence or absence of afflictions and the presence or absence of cultivation, one speaks of 'Buddha' or 'sentient being. Thus, although the essence is one, it is designated differently according to its mode of existence. This is the meaning of the teaching of Consciousness-Only.

Although there is no difference in the essence of this body and its land, they are distinguished because that which belongs to the Buddha and that which belongs to the Dharma-nature have different characteristics.

That is to say, when the Dharma-nature belongs to the Buddha, it is called the Dharma-nature Body (*dharmatā-kāya*); when the Dharma-nature belongs to the Dharma, it is called the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). This is stated because the nature [of the Dharma-nature] varies according to its manifestations.

As for the claim that the *Mahāvaipulya* sūtras state that insentient things lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this is merely a teaching given from the perspective of the provisional gate (*upāya-mukha*).
This statement is incorrect. Even if one were to go beyond this to the very last and ultimate proclamation of Nirvāṇa, it would still be only this teaching.
Because the nature (xing) differs according to its manifestations (xiang), one speaks of existence and non-existence; because they follow one another in arising, all things exist.
To claim that Nirvāṇa is taught through the provisional gate is a profound misinterpretation of the meaning of the sūtras.

The *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel) states: "How can one use the 'enabling' (*yuan*) and 'understanding' (*liao*) natures of Buddhahood—which are the fruits of wisdom (*zhi*) and severance (*duan*)—to challenge the 'direct cause' (*zhengyin*)?
Since the Tathāgata is the fruit of wisdom and Nirvāṇa is the fruit of severance, the nature of enabling and understanding exists upon these fruits of wisdom and severance.
Therefore, Kāśyapa raised the objection: 'The Tathāgata, the Buddha-nature, and Nirvāṇa exist. People of the world frequently cite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to raise such challenges."
Therefore, I have cited these at length to stifle further debate. You have not seen the passages on *nirvāṇa* and yet you vainly emulate the worldly obstruction of tiles and stones;

since the conditions of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) are difficult to rectify, they do not correspond [to your view]. This is precisely because you do not understand whether the Buddha-nature is advancing or regressing.

Furthermore, using emptiness as a metaphor for the *samyak* (correct), *pratyaya* (condition), and *niṣpatti* (perfection) is still too restrictive, just as Kāśyapa’s citation shows that all three are likewise [limited].
As for the statement that "it exists," this is because Nirvana is taught there as a provisional means (*upāya*).

The critique states: Although Nirvana is not what our school primarily venerates, it is certainly not the case that the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*) and "Conditioned Cause" (*yuan-yin*) are not present therein;

the fact that Nirvana possesses these True and Conditioned Causes is very clearly evident in the texts. Therefore, this is an error in the formulation of the thesis, resulting in a distorted interpretation.

To explain that the "conditions" (*pratyaya*) and "causes" (*hetu*) are categorized as provisional gates, and furthermore to treat the text with such literalism, results in a proliferation of secondary phrases that obscure the primary principle.
Now, I shall provide a brief indication so that the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* may manifest of itself. In the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa*, the Lion’s Roar poses this objection:
"As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas have two kinds of causes: first, the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*); [second, the indirect cause...]"
Regarding the two causes: the conditional cause takes the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) as the true cause of Buddha-nature; thus, "non-existence" is itself the true cause.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "To realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent—this realization is the revealing cause.
It is clearly known that although all sentient beings possess the wisdom of the emptiness of the ultimate truth...
If the nature of wisdom lacked *prajñā* as its revealing cause (*pariniṣpādaka-hetu*), it would ultimately never achieve Buddhahood or *nirvāṇa*.
(28) Furthermore, it says: "Good son, there are two kinds of causes: first, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); second, the revealing cause (*pariniṣpādaka-hetu*).
That which can produce a phenomenon is called the productive cause; a lamp that can illuminate objects is called the revealing cause. [The same applies to] the various fetters of affliction."

This is called the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). The parents of sentient beings are called the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*). A grain seed is called the productive cause, while soil and water are called the revealing cause.

The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are called the productive cause, and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is called the revealing cause. Because the six perfections can produce bodhi, they are the productive cause of bodhi;
because the Buddha-nature can reveal bodhi, it is the revealing cause of bodhi. Furthermore, it is said: "O son of good family..."
There are two kinds of causes: first, the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); second, the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). The direct cause is like milk producing curd;
the contributory cause is like yeast, warmth, and so forth. Since the unconditioned is not perceived, the direct cause is not seen;
because space lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no contributory cause. The Buddha said: "Good son, if there were a fixed nature within milk, why would it require..."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, because there is an inherent nature (*dhātu*), one requires a causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Why is this? It is for the sake of clear vision. A causal condition is precisely a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*). World-Honored One, it is like when various objects already exist in the darkness;
one uses a lamp to illuminate them so they may be seen. If they did not exist originally, what would the lamp illuminate?"
Just as because there is a jar within clay, human effort, water, a wheel, a cord, and a staff must serve as its *vijñapti-hetu* (causes of manifestation);

therefore, although the nature (*dhātu*) exists beforehand, it must depend on causes of manifestation before it can be seen. For this reason, one knows with certainty that the nature of curd already exists within milk;
although the essence of that nature exists, it must rely upon causes of manifestation and cultivation to be made manifest for sentient beings.
One cannot say that Buddha-nature is definitively existent or definitively non-existent. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, chapter thirty-five, states:
"To say that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature is called attachment; to say they do not possess Buddha-nature is called falsehood.
A wise person should say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings both exists and does not exist. Furthermore, Buddha-nature has four gates.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; it is like milk having the nature of curd.
This is the gate of existence (*yǒumén*). It further states: "Stone has no nature of gold, and milk has no nature of curd;
the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space—the emptiness of Kapilavastu and the Great Nirvāṇa are themselves the gate of emptiness (*kōngmén*). Furthermore, it says: "The multitude..."
Regarding the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, it both exists and does not exist. Why is it said to exist? Because all sentient beings equally possess it.
Why is it said not to exist? Because it is seen only through skillful means; this is the gate of both existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Middle Way: it is not existent like empty space, nor is it nonexistent like... [the remainder of the passage is omitted].

The hundred negations regarding the horns of a rabbit dispel this; this is the gate of "neither existence nor non-existence. If one consults the sūtras and śāstras, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) mostly elucidates the gate of existence;
the *Mādhyamakahṛdaya-vṛtti-tarkajvālā* (Pal-zhen) mostly analyzes the gate of emptiness; the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* (Zhongbian lun) mostly analyzes the gate of both existence and non-existence;
and the *Śataśāstra* (Zhongbai lun) mostly analyzes the gate of neither existence nor emptiness. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 36, states:
"Good son, if there is someone who says that all sentient beings definitely possess Buddha-nature, you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
If there is someone who says that all sentient beings definitely lack Buddha-nature, you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Since Nirvana is fully explained as consisting of the two causes—the direct cause and the contributing conditions—how can one [dismiss] the contributing conditions?"
I have therefore judged that the essential meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra has not been fully exhausted; the analogy of the lamp and its wick makes this principle very clear.
Should there be a public consensus on this, the dispute will naturally subside.

The *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel) states: "If the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) were not awakened, awakening would not be established; if there were no Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) that is not non-awakened, how could it be posited?
Thus, while the Buddha-nature as dharma-nature may be accommodated within the Lesser Vehicle, it is only when the dharma-nature is [revealed as] Buddha-nature that it is called the Great Teaching.

Therefore, I now ask you: among the various sūtras and śāstras, are the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the true nature (*tathatā*), and so forth, identical to the dharma-nature?

Regarding the division into two schools based on whether insentient things are identical with True Suchness (*tathatā*): if they were identical with True Suchness, one would not find such terms as "the dharma-realm of insentient things" or "the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the various sutras.

Furthermore, if insentient things were merely called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) and not "Buddha-nature," why does the *Gāthā-stava-parivarta* (Chapter on Verses of Praise) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, at the summit of Mount Sumeru, state: "One thoroughly understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent"?
If one can understand it in this way, then one sees Vairocana; is it not the case that all dharmas inherently possess the nature of Vairocana?

The critique states: If one says that awakening does not exist because there is no awakening within the dharma-nature, then how could the Buddha-nature—which is neither awakening nor non-awakening—be established?
The term "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) refers to the specific intrinsic nature of all phenomena; it is spoken of in relation to insentient things.

"Awakening" and "non-awakening," however, are spoken of in relation to sentient beings. Therefore, the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "Ordinary beings are said to be non-awakened; Bodhisattvas are said to be partially awakened;
and Tathāgatas are called ultimately awakened. How, then, can one say that dharmatā does not constitute Buddha-nature?

Furthermore, some say that the *dharmadhātu*, the *bhūtakoṭi*, the *tathatā*, and the *dharmatā* are identical; yet others claim that while these exist as the *dharmatā* within insentient things, they are distinct from *tathatā*.
Regarding this, Master Zhaolun stated: "The *mūla-abhāva*, the *tathatā*, the *dharmatā*, and the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) are but one meaning, being the convergence of conditions.
How can you take the identity of the *tathatā* with the *dharmatā* as a point of contention?
The questioner further asks: "If it is said that they are identical to True Suchness (tathatā), how can they be divided into two schools? The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

'True Suchness is precisely the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm; the Dharma-realm of True Suchness is as the principle is—empty, harmonious, equal, and non-dual.
How then can it be said that it is divided into two schools? Furthermore, you cite the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to prove the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
Because Buddha-nature is one, it is asked: "Is it not the case that the nature of *sāmbhogakāya* (She-na) is inherently present in all phenomena?

Since the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is often not the primary scripture or treatise under discussion, this point is treated quite briefly. Qingliang said: "When deluded emotions are shattered and principle manifests, one perceives *sāmbhogakāya*;
because nature fuses with form, there is no distinction between internal and external. How then can one say that [Buddha-nature] is merely among "all phenomena"?

Regarding the nature of the original *sambhogakāya* (she-na), the *Kongmu* states: "As for what is called 'Buddha-nature,' it is based on the term 'awakening' (*jue*). When one speaks of a 'Buddha,' it means awakening.

Yet, when one refers to insentient things (*wuqing*), one further says they possess awakening. If it were as you claim, then the sentient would transform into the insentient and the insentient would transform into the sentient;
this is largely equivalent to false views."
The *Jinbi* (Golden Scalpel) says: "I wish to open and guide your sentiments; therefore, I shall question you further with forty-six questions.
If you can understand even one of my questions, then all your obstructions will naturally dissolve, and the Dharma-realm will become integrated.

You will attain a vast and clear vision, seeing that within a single thought-moment, the Dharmadhātu—including both sentient beings and Buddhas, as well as their environments and bodies—is fully present without lacking even a single atom."
The critique states: Indeed, the essential meaning of Buddha-nature must be understood. Now, this school of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as its principle;
thus, by taking *dharmatā* as Buddha-nature, it is neither internal nor external. Depending on whether sentient beings are deluded or awakened, one may forcibly speak of their ascent or descent.
This school that takes *dharmatā* as its principle regards the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* as its tenet; therefore, *dharmatā* is itself the Buddha.
By nature, one knows that all phenomena are the very self-nature of the mind. If the mind-nature lacked Buddha-nature, there would be no phenomenon that was not the mind-nature;

thus, there would be no separation between internal and external, for the essence is neither internal nor external. Internal and external belong to the realm of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas the nature (*dharmatā*) is not like its characteristics.

How could characteristics possess internal or external? Yet, through delusion regarding this single nature, it transforms into what is "external. Since the external is ultimately nothing but mind, how can it be so?

There are things not transformed by the Buddha that lack substantial reality; therefore, it is said that walls and such have no Buddha-nature. Yet, since the nature (svabhāva) encompasses the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), there is nothing that is not of the nature.

Just as smoke arises from fire and smoke is thus fire, or as waves are formed from water and waves are thus water, so too objects arise through the transformation of the mind and objects are not different from the mind.
If the mind possesses nature, how could objects not possess it? How much more so the mind itself!

Both the subject and its object are identical to true nature (*dharmatā*), and since true nature is non-dual, how could mind and object be at odds? If one follows nature through its forms, there is no hindrance to the internal and external;

yet, if one uses external objects as an analogy for the mind, requiring it to possess conscious awareness and engage in cultivation to become a Buddha, this is the dharma of heterodox paths and false views.
Therefore, one must constantly illuminate [the mind] as being neither identical to nor separate from [objects], neither one with them nor distinct from them.
There is no difference, and thus there is no delusion.
The *Golden Scalpel* states: "The first question asks about the name 'Buddha-nature': does it proceed from cause or from fruit? If it proceeds from cause, it is not Buddha;
if it is the fruit, it is not called 'nature'."
The commentary states: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says that Buddha-nature has the cause and the cause of the cause, as well as the fruit and the fruit of the fruit.
The "cause" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination; the "cause of the cause" refers to wisdom; the "fruit" refers to great bodhi;
and the "fruit of the fruit" refers to great nirvāṇa. Since these four are all termed Buddha-nature, the first two are inherently existent.
Regarding the latter two [points], the logic and textual evidence are perfectly clear; how can it be difficult to say that [the result] arises from causes?
To claim that the Buddha-fruit is not called "nature" (dhātu) is erroneous.
At the very end of the *Jinbi*, there is one question which asks the practitioner to contemplate the mind, the mind-Buddha, sentient beings, cause and effect, and the bodies and lands of the Dharma.
Are all things mutually inclusive and identical? The critique states:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. The mind is the general characteristic;

when awakened, it is called the Buddha and constitutes pure dependent origination; when deluded, it becomes sentient beings and constitutes defiled dependent origination. Thus, there is defilement and purity.

Although the functions differ, the essence of the mind is one; this explains how the mind universally pervades and encompasses all things. Why then is it used as proof that the characteristics of the body and the land are entirely identical?
The *Jinpi* states: A visitor asked, "For what reason is there neither more nor less than forty-six [categories]? I replied: "To attack delusions and to attack [them thoroughly]."

Whether attacking through doubt, attacking through practice, or through the penetration of principle, the penetration of teaching, and the penetration of meaning—whether penetrating for oneself or for others—a single question is sufficient to serve as a response.
Because of those with dull faculties, there are forty-six [types of questions] to be known; yet one should understand that each single question is also capable of being an attack.
The commentary states: "If one can refute [the argument] by refuting only the beginning, the end, and the middle, then all forty-six questions may likewise be refuted.
Why? Because he employs 'one thought-moment encompassing the three thousand' to extend his response to the forty-six questions;

this includes cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, sentient beings and Buddhas—all phenomena whatsoever—and since even the subsequent passages are all based on this same principle."

I do not offer a critique; rather, I have merely followed the principle that "nature conforms to characteristics" (*xing cong xiang*), yet I have not yet fully understood the teaching that "characteristics conform to nature" (*xiang cong xing*).
Consequently, even such things as walls, bricks, and rubble are relegated to the periphery of the gate of authority. Students should abandon their emotional attachments to these views;

however, the Sage’s intent is profound and remote, and each person, according to their own capacity for understanding, may grasp it and express their own perspective to collectively praise the Great Way.
Written on the day of the tenth month in the Jia-yin year of the Shaoxi era by the Bhikṣu Shanxi of Yigan.

On the twenty-second day of the eighth month in the fifth year of Kenchō, at the hour of Si (10–11 a.m.), at Katsuragi on the outskirts of Hana-shita.
I have dyed purple brushes at the waves of the Seiryō River and ground white hemp paper on the mists of Takao Mountain.
Having dispelled the doubts and obscurities of later students, I have transcribed this new translation of the *Tángshū* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra). This dedication is without duality;

it is solely for the flourishing of the Huayan Buddha-dharma, and my aspiration is for nothing other than the fulfillment of the rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven. May the Triple Gem of this one school [grant their blessings].
I merely pray that you will look upon us with compassion and grant that these virtuous vows for the welfare of both worlds may be fulfilled. The śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (secular age thirty-two;
seventeen years since receiving the precepts), on the ninth day of the ninth month in the year of Kyōwa 11, Jiaxu, happened upon this rare manuscript and could not restrain his joy at its discovery.

This student has transcribed this compilation based on his own collation of manuscripts; as it contains passages not seen by the late Master Fūtan Tokumon, it should be kept secret, it should be kept secret.
